title: Felix and the Weather
premise: Beatrix Blackwood has spent thirty years as the family's invisible middle daughter, inspecting bridges by day and measuring her own marriage in hairline cracks. At her father's funeral, a stranger named Felix Okafor addresses the family by their true surname—Blackwood-Adjei—revealing that her father secretly co-owned the old neighborhood rowhouse with Felix's late mother, and left it to both families jointly. As the bus route to the fading neighborhood is permanently rerouted, Beatrix must choose between preserving the family's carefully arranged silence and claiming the inheritance—and the truth—that would finally make her visible. She ends the marriage, signs the deed with Felix, and rides the last bus down the old route one final time.
about_author: Tamsin Ravensworth is a former municipal surveyor who spent a decade documenting disappearing infrastructure across northern England before turning to fiction. She writes about the quiet violence of families and the mathematics of things that hold.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV at her father's funeral, where she performs grief flawlessly while cataloguing the cracks in her marriage to Richard like expansion joints on a failing span. Her sister controls the eulogy; her mother arranges mourners like furniture. Then Felix Okafor appears at the graveside and calls the family 'Blackwood-Adjei,' a name nobody uses. Emotional beat: the first fracture in a lifetime of practiced invisibility—curiosity overriding the smile.

chapters.title: What the Deed Knows
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV as she tracks Felix to the old neighborhood and discovers the joint deed: her father and Felix's mother bought the rowhouse together decades ago, partners in something unrecorded. Her mother denies everything with terrifying calm; Richard urges her to sign away her share for peace. Emotional beat: rising tension as Beatrix realizes the family's arrangement was built to bury not just a property but a whole history of love against duty.

chapters.title: Last Bus Before the Rerouting
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Beatrix and Felix on the day the council reroutes the 47 bus forever. They ride the old route together while Felix tells her what his mother never could: the two elders loved each other and chose their duties instead. Beatrix confronts Richard, who confesses he always knew she was somewhere else even in the same bed. Emotional beat: climax—the question the family arranged itself around is finally asked aloud: who were they, really?

chapters.title: Load-Bearing
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, weeks later. The marriage ends without spectacle; the family scatters into honest, smaller shapes. She and Felix co-sign the deed, keeping the rowhouse as an archive of the truth rather than a monument to silence. Standing on the bridge she inspects, she measures it differently now—not for failure but for what holds. Emotional beat: resolution—justice outside the law, love claimed late but claimed, and visibility chosen over safety.
